Here, the authors use collective-coordinate optimization to build two-dimensional disk packings that are polycrystalline yet ultradense, stealthy, and hyperuniform. Compared with dense, nonhyperuniform polycrystalline packings produced by standard compression algorithms, their packings show a distinctive grain-size distribution reflecting long-range grain correlations, perfect transparency to electromagnetic waves at small wave vectors, and enhanced diffusion spreadability. Although unlikely to form naturally, they could be realized through nanolithography or 3D printing as optical and transport metamaterials.

Proton–boron-11 (p–11B) fusion only converts its reactants into three charged α particles, so that is an attractive aneutronic path to fusion energy, but the high Coulomb barrier of the 11B nucleus (Z = 5) keeps its reactivity low. We study a new pathway that form a muonic hydrogen atom (pμ) first, whose Bohr radius is about 200 times smaller than ordinary hydrogen, then bombard it with a 11B nucleus. We simulate the full three-body classical motion with the classical trajectory Monte Carlo method, sampling the pμ initial state from the microcanonical ground-state ensemble. From the statistical distribution of classical turning points, we compute the Coulomb-barrier tunneling probability and obtain the cross section. The results show that the μ enhances the low-energy cross section by several orders of magnitude compared with bare nuclei. Thus, if combined with intense laser fields or high-density compression, this mechanism may enable low-energy auxiliary ignition of aneutronic p–11B fusion.

To date, approaches for bringing the Fermi level into alignment with a VHS have relied mainly upon gating, chemical doping, or heterostructure engineering. Here, the authors demonstrate an alternative pathway - combining topological insulators (antimony telluride) with topological semimetals (antimonene) in the form of antimony telluride homologous superlattices. They identify the key role of Sb and Te pz orbital hybridization in generating the saddle point and shifting it toward the Fermi level as the number of antimonene layers increases. In a Fermi liquid, the quasiparticle scattering rate scales as T2, whereas the low-temperature correction to the residual resistivity can scale as T4, seemingly implying a strongly suppressed current-relaxation rate. They show that electron–electron collisions enter the conductivity through the quasiparticle scattering time itself, which controls the crossover between collisionless and hydrodynamic transport. The extra T2 factor arises because momentum conservation makes the change in the total velocity of two colliding electrons vanish on the Fermi surface, so current relaxation comes only from thermally excited states away from it. The electron–electron contribution to the dc conductivity nevertheless remains parametrically small throughout the Fermi-liquid regime. By extrapolating the result toward a z=3 quantum critical point, the authors further show that the renormalized quasiparticle scattering rate saturates the Planckian bound.
